utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Prosecutor, or madam Prosecutor, you have the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the next witness, the witness has indicated she wishes to testify openly. Therefore, I ask that the protective order be lifted ----- (Technical difficulties with interpreters' channels)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] Yes, Miss McHenry, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. The next witness, your Honour, has indicated she wishes to testify publicly, so with respect to this witness I ask that the protective order be lifted other than for the witness's address.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] The Registrar will take note of the lifting of that non-disclosure order with the exception, of course, in regard of the witness's address which means that the witness will testify publicly as has been requested. The witness has then been informed of all the rights of protection which the International Criminal Tribunal is able to provide. That having been done, I would suggest you ask the clerk to bring in the witness. You can pass that information on to the witness that has just been given.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Zehra Smajlovic. ZEHRA SMAJLOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Madam Smajlovic, first of all, can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] No, I cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] Can you hear now, Mrs. Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Yes, I can hear you now

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] Please remain standing just the time to read out the solemn declaration for the Tribunal. If you would kindly read that in your language, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] A bit louder, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] Can you hear, Mrs. Smajlovic? Mrs. Smajlovic, the International Criminal Tribunal which is prosecuting the perpetrators of crimes against humanity is here to hear your testimony which the Prosecutor's office thought was appropriate to hear in connection with the case against Dragan Nikolic. We are very appreciative of you being here today and, as for other witnesses, we realise what this involves for you, to come here and tell us about things you have seen, heard, all of the things you have been through, your suffering, and which you are going to try to express to us in your own words. So we are very appreciative of you being here. We are going to be listening very carefully to everything you have to say. You should speak in a peaceful state of mind. This is a place where justice is administered. Feel at home in so far as possible. If you have any problems at any point in time, please do not hesitate to tell us. The Judges, the Tribunal, so far as possible, will do what they can to help you. You have the floor, Miss McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): Ma'am, would you please state you full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Zehra Smajlovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old are you, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 61 -- 63, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Smajlovic, if you have any trouble hearing the interpretation when I am asking questions, please just tell us because we can adjust the volume of your microphone. Is that all right? If at any point during your testimony you would like to take a break, please just let us know that also and I am sure the Judges would take a break. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Smajlovic, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you live in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 59 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live with your family in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was part of your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family is in Tuzla now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was part of your family in Vlasenica? Who did you live with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived with my husband, with my son. I had two sons. I had a daughter too. One of my sons is in Tuzla, and one of my sons used to live with me in Vlasenica and my daughter got married in a village near Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that the court has heard testimony from a Mirsad Smajlovic; is he any relation to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he any relation to your husband

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What relation is he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is my -- he is the son of my husband's brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you tell the court what happened in Vlasenica in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened on the 15th, between the 10th and the 15th April. Milorad (Lukic) came -- he is from the Serbian party -- and he invited us to stay. He told us to stay in Vlasenica. He told us that we will not be touched and we would go on living together. After that a lot of us stayed, some of us left. Then on the 21st, the Yugoslav army came. The units that belonged to Vojvodina Corp., from Vojvodina, they took over Vlasenica together with the Serbs, local Serbs, from Vlasenica and the surrounding area. That is how in the next morning, around 3 o'clock, they entered the town, and when they got up the next morning we saw tanks in the streets, soldiers, and we also saw the local Serbo Chetniks, as we called them. They were together with them. They wore camouflage uniforms. They were masked. They had socks -- they wore socks on their heads and faces -- stockings on their faces. Then I left Drum. It is a local cemetery, local Muslim cemetery. That happened around the 25th April. I cannot recall the exact date but I went to our cemetery, the Muslim cemetery, and I saw a tank stationed there and which belonged to the Yugoslav army, to the Vojvodina Corps I went there. I passed there. I saw it. I saw the tank and I was stopped and they asked me: "Where are you going, grandma?" I told them: "Well, I want to go over there. I have some family over there". Then they said: "What is this happening here? No-one is shooting, not a single bullet has been shot and they, the Serbian party, they called us. They invited us here. They told us that allegedly Muslims were slaughtering Serbs in Vlasenica, but here we realised that not a single bullet had been shot. We have been cheated". A soldier told me that and he told me not to go there. He said: "Go back. You will be better over there." I did not know that soldier. He wore a helmet on his head and also an olive green uniform and he was dressed for the tank. So I went back, and in front of the Ministry of the Interior building I saw a lot of soldiers around there, a lot of soldiers belonging to the Yugoslav army, and also some local Serbo Chetniks. I saw them standing there. They asked for identity papers. They did not ask me anything so I went back home. That is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the soldiers from Vojvodina, what towns are part of Vojvodina, in particular is -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We do not know. They did not tell us. He did not tell me. He did not tell me where he was from. He just said that they belonged to the Vojvodina Corps., Vojvodanskih Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the Vojvodina Corps. do you know the relationship between the Vojvodina and Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that Novi Sad is in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point did the soldiers from the JNA army leave

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, they stayed there a while. I do not know how long, how many days they stayed there, but probably between 10 and 15 days, but we could not move around a lot; we were not allowed to. So later on they went. They left. Those, the Serbo Chetniks, while they were there, they already starting taking men to the police building. They took them for interrogation. Then they released some of them, some of them were held. Then they left. I do not remember the exact day they left. I did not move around a lot because I was not allowed to. Later on when I went to buy cigarettes I saw that they had tanks. I realised that they had left weapons to them, and near the Panorama Hotel there were tanks around the hotel as well, and the tanks were also near the cemetery. The tanks stayed and the soldiers had left. They left the tanks to the Serbo Chetniks. Then they started to arrest people, to evict people. They started taking people to the camps. I was once chased away from my home and then one of them, a soldier, told me: "Grandma, go back to your house; you will not be touched. You can go on living freely." Then they took other people to the camp. There was Mahmutovic Mina, Mirsad's wife, who had a sick child and the soldier told her: "You can stay home with your sick child. You are young. You can take care of the grandma". The next day Mina left. Her husband had been taken to the camp, and then she left the camp as well. I stayed alone. I went back to my house from Mina's house. So I stayed there for a while. Then I also started hiding because I thought tha some people would be left alone in the town, but then they did not. They took many people to the camp. I stayed in my house for a while. Then Aco Djuric arrived, Pero's son, and also Sinisa Miljanic and Elvis Djuric, Aco's brother, and they started to take us away from our homes. I went to Kicic Huma, her husband was there too. He was hiding. Aco approached them and he started to beat her husband. He started to beat her too and I told him: "Aco, do not do it. You know that you used to live together with my cousin. You grew up together. Your mother is a Muslim. Do not do that. It is not good what you are doing. You can have pity on us." So he went to me and then kicked me twice here and I had bruises all over. He told me: "If you tell anyone about this, I will kill you, I will kill you on the spot." So I did not say anything. So we went to the camp and that is how we arrived at the camp. First, they did not let us in the camp. We waited outside a little bit. We saw three buses there, buses that they used to take people to Batkovic, towards Bijeljina, only Muslim men. There I recognised a lot of people I knew, children of the people I knew from my neighbourhood, from my street. I recognised Mirsad, Nurija, Hasim -- there were many of them, I cannot remember all of them -- Suljo Mujanovic, Djemel Mujanovic. I recognised them as they were on the bus and that is how they stood. They had to put their hands behind their heads. Then the soldiers left and then we were taken inside the camp. Then in the camp I saw some women -- yes

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I go back for a minute? First of all ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- going back to the time when you were still in the town, before you were brought to the camp, did you have any discussions with anyone about the existence of a Crisis Committee, Kruzni Stab, in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was -- I got confused a little bit. I apologise. This is the first time for me here. I forgot to tell you about Olja. Olja was our neighbour and I remember him passing, walking with his wife and he told me: "Hello, Zehra", and I told him: "Hello, Olja. Olja, what is going on here? How come your wife is so nicely dressed?" He said: "Well, she is working in the Crisis Committee". I said: "What kind of Crisis Committee is that? Where is it? How come it cannot protect us?" Then he said: "I do not know anything about it. It is in the Bauxite company". It was located on the outskirts of Vlasenica. Then he said: "That is where it is." So I said: "What do you think of this?" He said: "I do not know. I cannot tell you anything. I am not allowed to tell you anything." I tried again to ask him to help me somehow. I wanted to ask him if he could help me get on the bus and not end up in the camp, if I could somehow leave for the -- on that bus. He said: "Well, you can try", and that is what I did. I went to the bus station and I saw many people standing there. They were putting them on the bus and they told me: "Grandma, go back home. Do not go anywhere. You are not going to be touched. I can guarantee you that. I will take care of you. I wil visit you from time to time. Do not worry." So I went back to my home and I stayed there until Aco took me away from my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversation with Olja about people detained in Susica camp and asking why they were being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. He did not tell me that. He was not allowed to. He just kept silent. I realised that he did not mean anything. He was not malicious, but he just kept silent. They were not allowed to talk to us, to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were brought to Susica, when Aco came to your house, were you brought to Susica voluntarily? In other words, did you want to go or were you taken there forcibly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was forced to. He beat me, yes, he kicked me with his shoes here. I had bruises all over. I just had to; we were forced to go. They were beating us as we were leaving our houses and they just took all the people from the street and then they took us to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what time this was that you were taken to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the 30th June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other people were taken with you to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 20 people, 20 women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people from the same street that you lived on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but also from other streets from the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who brought you to Susica, were they local soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were locals, all neighbours

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had olive green uniforms. Aco had one and Elvis too, Sinisa Miljanic had his jeans on and black jacket on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to go to the time period when you were brought to the camp. Can you describe when you were brought inside, the physical structure of the camp and where you were brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a large room with some 20 metres long and some 15 metres wide. When we were -- the door was very large. The building was called the hangar and it had a very large door through which we entered, and through which people would also leave. I can only say that as soon as I entered I saw there women children, men, many men; I cannot tell you how many. It is very difficult to decide how many people there were. We were all very frightened and could not think calmly or we could not count but there was a large number of people. When I entered there I saw Fikret Arnaut and Cece, nicknamed Cece. He was sitting on the concrete floor. He was swollen. I looked at him and said: "Cice, what happened?" He said: "Look at me and you will see". He said: "Give me a glass of water" and somebody said, somebody came to him to give him water because at the corner of the building next to the door there was a can of water, and she was -- she tried to give him water but then the soldier said: "No, I kill you if you do that", so she turned back without giving him the water. So the evening came and then this devil came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to that, Mrs. Smajlovic, can I ask you couple of other general questions about the camp? In particular, do you have any idea about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- how many women were at the camp when you arrived there besides your group of 20 women and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There would be some 50 women, if not more. I honestly say I could not count and there were lots of children as well, lots of children, and quite a number of women. I cannot give you the exact figure, because I did not count and we were not even allowed to look around too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there more men than women in the camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. There were many more men than women, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were brought to the camp was any property taken from any of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at once. At first they did not take anything but later they did. Later they did, two or three days later. This devil, Nikolic, told us, he entered the building, he shouted, cursing our Muslim mothers. He had a cigarette in his hand and he said: "Look, listen, you are less worth for me than this cigarette butt. This cigarette butt is more valuable than you are. Anybody who has anything on them, cigarettes, matches, gold, anything, please throw it on to the floor into the centre of the hangar, of the room", and so they did, people did that. I did not have anything. I only threw my packet of cigarettes and the lighter, cigarette lighter. When all of this was on the floor, he called two people, two detainees, asking them to collect all of these objects. He brought two buckets and they put it -- pu the objects into the buckets. They took it outside in front of the door and came back. What happened with these objects later, we do not know. Whether it was for himself or whether it was for somebody else, we do not know because he closed the door of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any record made of what property each detainee was turning over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all, nothing. Nobody made any record. No record was made, nor was there an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not this property was ever returned to the people to whom it belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never, never. Nobody ever had anything returned that had been taken away from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said there were other women there, were you the oldest woman who was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw another woman that was older than me. She must have been 75 years old, maybe 80. That was Hacic, the woman's name was Hacic, but I forget her first name now. She was also in the detention room. Then later she wanted to go to the toilet, they would not allow her, and then Dragan Nikolic came and said: "Bind her", so they bound her hands and feet. They tied ropes around her hands and feet so that she could not actually go to the toilet and she had to urinate in the room where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know at any time while you were at the camp was there a woman named Hasna Cakisic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She was brought after me, some 12 days after me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how old she was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that she was 65, not more than that, I should say, 65 years old. Again I cannot judge very well bu I know her, I know her family, but I never asked her exactly how old she was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Inside the camp were the women kept -- can you describe where the women were kept versus where the men were kept, and if there were any areas within that big room used for special purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me try to describe this. This is the hangar, the large, large room, the hangar. One side -- men were on one side, the other side, the corner, was empty and we all women were on this side, and there were buckets in the other corner which were used for urination and defecation. This was our toilet, if you like. At the far end were people who were being beaten and when Nikolic decided who he would beat there were people by these buckets and they were taken out to be beaten then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to Nikolic, do you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikolic Dragan was his name. His father was -- oh, I forget the name of his father now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dragan Nikolic before you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I used to know him. I used to see a lot of him. I knew his father and mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Dragan Nikolic's role in the camp was, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us himself. He said: "I am the commander of this camp. You should know that there is nobody above me." That is what he told us in front of everybody. He said: "I am your God and you have no other God but me"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were starting to tell us, Mrs. Smajlovic, about what happened the first night you were at the camp when Dragan Nikolic came in, I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he walked in. Dragan Nikolic, he shouted and yelled, swore at, swore our Muslim mothers, cursed, said: "You should know that I am the one who is responsible for this outfit. I am responsible for you. You are in my hands. I can do what I like." Then he approached Fikret Arnaut and then he took him out, started beating him in front of the hangar. The door was open. He had a bandage on his hand and something dark on the fingers. I do not know what it is because I am not familiar with these objects, but there was first a bandage on the fingers and then something very dark on his fingers. The man who was beaten started crying for help, for mercy. Then he took two other prisoners, Agic, Rasim Agic, his son I mean, but I have forgotten the name now and Alija Ferhatovic, Muharem, the son of Muharem Ferhatovic. These two were called out to pour water out of a bucket over this man that was lying there. Then we saw that Dragan was removing his bandages and in front of the hangar there was the guard house and Zija was taken there from the hangar to help the guards, to work for them. She also poured water for Dragan. He washed his hands. She gave him the towel. Then she came -- he came back into the hangar, came to Fikret Arnaut and started kicking him with his feet and shoes. This was like a rabid dog. You could not watch that. The screams were horrible to hear and cries for mercy. Then Dragan would leave and the door was locked. Th door was closed again and that is the way it was. That is the way it was from the first night on when we came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just described, as I understand you, the first night when Dragan Nikolic beat Cece Arnaut. After that first night, did you ever see ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Cece Arnaut beaten at any other time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was every night. Every night for two times as long as I stayed there in the camp for 20 days. Every night the same punishment, the same beating. He was completely broken. He was being dragged out, then dragged from outside back into the hangar, and this was done by the detainees who had to do this. Ferhatovic and Agic, they were -- they poured water over him and were then forced to drag him back into the hangar. So, he was a very strong and powerful man, and he said: "I cannot go on like this." Then Nikolic said: "I cannot kill this manure". He would curse his Muslim mother and it went on. It was repeated on and on, again and again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a man named Ismet Dedic at the camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about Ismet Dedic? Do you know where he was from or where he lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from Gerovi. Gerovi is some 15 kilometres away from Vlasenica, maybe not even 15, 10 kilometres. I cannot tell you exactly. I know his family because my daughter is married there in Gerovi and he used to work in the Bauxite company. He got a flat in Vlasenica and h lived there with his wife and children. He was a nice man. I know him -- I knew him. He was brought to the camp and each night and each day, they just kept bringing more people to the camp from the town, from the surrounding villages, so the camp was getting full. So he approached Dedic. Dedic was sitting at that moment with his head bent down. He told him: "You are a very nice man" and then he walked out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the time you saw Nikolic say to Mr. Dedic that he was a nice man, did you ever see any other contact between Dragan Nikolic and Mr. Dedic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything happen to Mr. Dedic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After he had said that he went out and then he came back again, and again he had those bandages on his hand and he had the black finger on his hand again. He went to Dedic and he kicked him and then Dedic got up, and followed Nikolic out. Then he started beating him, stomping on him with his military boots on. He beat him so much you could not recognise him any longer. So then he came back in the hangar, and he called Ferhatovic and Agic. He called them out. So they went out. Then they brought Dedic in and put in the punishment corner inside the hangar. You could not recognise Dedic's eyes, mouth. He had blood all over his face. So he gurgled a little bit in that corner for maybe one hour, hour and a half, and then he died. Then other prisoners knocked at the door and th guards opened the door, and then they threw inside a plastic bag. Then they wrapped him, wrapped Dedic, in the bag and they took him out. They stayed out for about 15 minutes and then they came back inside. We asked them: "What happened? Where did you bury him?" Then Ferhatovic just motioned, meaning he did not know anything. He was not allowed to say anything. He knew that he would share the same fate. That is what I know about Dedic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Ferhatovic motioned, which Ferhatovic are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Alija Ferhatovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you described when he was beating him and stamping on him, who is "he"? Who was beating Mr. Dedic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a man named Mevludin Hatunic at the camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like to take a break or would you like a glass of water, Mrs. Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am all right. I will drink water later, but I can speak now without drinking any water. So just continue, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Hatunic before you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He lived not far from me. We were all people from Vlasenica. I used to know them, I used to know their parents, their children, their wives. I knew everybody. He was a plumber, and he worked in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you observe with respect to Mr. Hatunic at the camp

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was -- they called him to repair the plumbing or water supply. He went. He worked for a day and he -- I cannot tell you which day that was. It is very difficult for me. I just cannot remember the dates and the days when things happened because in this horror we lost track of time. Anyway he came. He walked into the hangar, followed by Dragan Nikolic and Dragan Nikolic said: "Ah, you and I will go out now". So he took him out and beat him and beat him, and shouted: "What will you be singing and what have you been singing? You went there to a Serb and he offered brandy, you drank it and you said that your bird will sing one day." But he never said anything about any bird singing or anything. He did not say anything. Of course, he was not drunk. He knew what was happening and then he would not have done that. So, Nikolic took him out and beat him again with the bandaged hand, with a black object on it, and he hit him. The man cried for mercy, cried for help, and eventually when he fainted, he looked like dead. Then again Nikolic called Agic and Ferhatovic, Alija Ferhatovic. They came, they dragged him into the hangar and he started groping and turning around. You could not see his face properly because it was all disfigured and he was groping, came to Cece, to Bego. Bego took him, slowly put him to his punishment corner and so he was there for an hour or two. He gurgled. He suffocated and then he died. Ferhatovic and Agic came put on him on a stretcher, wrapped in a plastic bag, took him out and again they came back after 10 to 15 minutes. W knew that the burial must have been taking place somewhere not very far from the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also at the camp a man named Galib Music?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Music, beforehand do you know anything about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from Vlasenica. He was a born Vlasenica man, just like I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about how old Mr. Music was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say he was roughly 60, not more than 60. I would say 60, 61 or 2, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not before he was brought to the camp Mr. Music and Mr. Dragan Nikolic knew each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were actually first next door neighbour, first neighbours. Their houses were one next to the other and they knew each other very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you observe happen to Mr. Music while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He, Dragan Nikolic, came and Galib Music was seated smoking a cigarette. Dragan entered and called him out. Again on that occasion he had a bandaged hand plus that dark object. He took Galib out, Galib, and started beating him. Galib cried for mercy. Then he could not speak. Then he trampled him with his heavy shoes, beat him all over the body, the kidneys -- and this was impossible even to watch such a beating. Then again the same thing happened. Again he called Alija Ferhatovic and he called the other man. They came They dragged Galib into the hangar and he lived for no more than half an hour after that. He died. Somebody knocked on the door of the camp from the inside. The guards came, gave them a plastic bag or plastic something, put him on the stretcher and took him out and again came back fairly quickly, fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the camp, were you ever there when some visitors came from outside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a number came. Some five to six people would come with Dragan Nikolic, and then Dragan would say -- now, this was a van, a van or minibus, rather, with the company name of Elastik on it -- so they would come and Dragan would enter with them. On the first occasion when they arrived they took six or seven, seven people. He took them out in the morning, and they came back round 6 o'clock in the afternoon. They brought them back. They entered the hangar but Pasic did not come back, Ekrem Pasic, I think that was the name. I do not know his first name. He is not my next door neighbour, so he lived some distance from my house. So I know that his name was Pasic and I think it was Ekrem. Ekrem was probably his first name. He was not brought back. Then the door was closed. We asked: "Where is Ekrem?" They said: "He is no longer there. He does not exist any more". We knew that he was killed. Then Dragan started to shout in front of the camp. The door was ajar and you could hear everything that happened outside. Also, his voice was very strong and clear because he was yelling all the time. So he asked: "Where is he?" and the man came: "Oh, well, forget him." So I understoo that. I mean, Dragan Nikolic was asking about Ekrem, I am sure, and the other answered: "Well, you know, forget him" which means he had been killed. Later we learned that when he was taken there, then he said: "But do not say that to anybody, do not spread the word". I do not know who it was that said that. Somebody came to us women and said: "I was there. Dika Zubovic was there", because he was a friend of Dika Zubovic. He spoke about Ekrem and he came to her and said, I do not know his name, Ali Hodjic, I think, but I do not know the first name, and he said, well, they were digging a canal, a trench, or something, I do not know, and that he was a bit further away from the rest of the group and when they stepped out of the canal a shot was heard and they waited for Ekrem to appear. He did not appear and then they left. So they were told that Ekrem had been killed in that canal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the camp did anyone ever visit the camp who came on a helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no with helicopter. A helicopter flew over -- the door of the hangar was open. We were outside. We were eating. The helicopter flew over. I do not know who was there. They started shooting. The guards started shooting -- Nikolic as well -- and then Nikolic said: "Ah, this is our God over there in helicopter" but who was there, I do not know. I could not see who was in the helicopter because I was in the camp and he was in the helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the guards and Nikolic were shooting, do you mean they were shooting at the helicopter or they wer shooting for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at the helicopter, no, no. They were shooting for joy. The helicopter had flown away and they were so joyful that they thought they could celebrate by shooting. They were rejoicing seeing the helicopter and, as far as I know, the helicopter then landed in the Vlasenica football field.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the camp did you learn anything about some detainees delivering letters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was Nikolic who sent, first, Biba Hadzic who took a letter to Cerska sent by Nikolic while her two sons remained in the camp. Then the letter was an invitation or an order for Cerska to surrender. So then Biba left for Cerska. Then the Muslims, when she came to Cerska did not allow her to go back to the camp so we do not know exactly what happened, but later they sent Mejra Sabic and she was sent. She also left with the letter but never came back. Then Fata, Fata Osmanlic was sent, but none of them ever came back from Cerska to tell us exactly what happened. The Cerska authorities, our soldiers there, Muslim soldiers, did not allow her to go back to the camp, so they remained in Cerska until Cerska was occupied, but when Cerska was occupied they were brought to Tuzla, they came to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to at least the first letter that Biba Hadzic had, how do you know that the letter was an order for Cerska to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Her son told us that, that Biba had gone to Cerska, that she was sent with a letter asking, calling on Cerska to surrender. That is what I know

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately, if you know, how far away is Cerska from Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 25 kilometres perhaps, not more than that, 25 to 30, perhaps. 25, I think, is more like it. Between 25 and 30 kilometres. I am sorry, I cannot be precise. I know Cerska but I never worried about how many kilometres it was distance from Vlasenica. Roughly 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you released from Susica, Mrs. Smajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been the 19th or 20th July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances surrounding your release, how it worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nikolic came and he said: "I will send you to Kladanj, so that you can go over to your people, to Ustashas", that is how he called, how he called our army. So we waited there. He did not know who will be selected to go. It was around 6 o'clock in the afternoon. He came back again and he said: "You, you, you". He selected some people as he wanted and he had one truck and one bus. So it was my turn, and he told me: "Get up". So I got up and that is how we went. The bus was full and the truck was full as well, fully loaded. They loaded us as straw, but a lot of people were left behind, a lot of men, women and children. Then when we left the camp we reached their checkpoint first, and on that checkpoint we were ordered to get off the bus and the truck and then they started selecting young women, girls. The first one was only 14 and the second could have been 16 or 17, and then they selected other young girls. I knew them all. They were from Vlasenica. There were many young women there, youn and beautiful women, even some children. So they started separating them from us, older women, and putting them aside in the street. When that was over they selected about 20, 27 young women. You just could not watch and I could not tell how many they were. But I was so sorry for those young women, girls, children. One of them was a very young mother. She could have been 25. Two sisters they were, one of them was pregnant and one of them had a small child with her. The child was maybe three years old, not more than that, and they were also selected. Then they started yelling: "We want the Muslims to see what our seed is", that is what, the expression they used. Then they cursed us again, swore. You could not watch it. Mothers were crying. Their children were being separated and I stood aside. It was so hard for me and I started to cry. I had just left the camp, so I was very tired, very hungry and dirty. It was so difficult for me. There was a fence near the road and one of them, one of them, a soldier was standing there. He held a rifle in his hand and he said: "Grandma, stop. Do not cry. It is not my fault". I could see tears in his eyes and he said: "Grandma, please, do not cry. It is not my fault". Then I just kept silent. I bowed my head and I cried. Then he said: "Just walk straight in the middle of the road. Do not stray aside from the road because it is mined. So once you reach that place there is a hotel over there". It was in the wilderness. There is a forest over there and a river as well and we people fro Vlasenica, we used to go to that hotel before, and then he said: "When you reach the hotel there is no-one up there. Then you should speak very loud because it will be dark so as your people will not shoot to us because they will not know who is coming", and that is how we arrived there. It was difficult. There were many roads there, many logs on the road. It was completely dark and when we reached that place where our people were, they had to carry me. I could not walk any more, so they just carried me. Two young men who approached me, I do not know them, they carried me and then we arrived at Ravne where our soldiers were and then they called some buses, and that is how we arrived at Kladanj. I spent the night at Kladanj and the next day I was transported into Tuzla in a school building, and that is where I found my husband, my family, my children when I got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the young women who were taken away, did you ever see or hear from any of those young women again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. Never -- any of them. They are just no longer there. We know -- we know that, and Dragan Nikolic knows about it very well. That is what he did actually.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: I do not have any more questions for this witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] Mrs. Smajlovic, the Judges have several additional questions to put to you. We would suggest a break and we would resume at 11.30. You will come back because, as I have said, the Judges do have several questions for you. That way, you can make the most of th break. We have our witness assistance facilities here, the people have been taking care of you since you have come to The Hague. So during this break you will be seen to and we will resume in 20 minutes at 11.30. The meeting is adjourned. (Short Adjournment) (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] Prosecution, please, before giving you the floor, I would like to ask Mrs. Smajlovic how she is feeling, if she is feeling all right? Did you rest a little bit, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am feeling all right. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: : [Original in French] You have the floor, m'am.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Smajlovic, is there anything besides what you have asked you and what you have already testified to that you would like to tell your Honours about what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you not please tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was in the camp, Dragan Nikolic came on 10th July and he took 12 men Muslim, 12 Muslim men, and said: "They are going to cut grass", but these men never came back to the camp. They never returned, nor have they ever sent word of their whereabouts to anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who any of these men were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was there somebody called Hasanovic, Hajro called, nicknamed Hane, but I do not remember his second name. There was a man called Hasanovic then Bego Topcic, Ali Hodjic, Mustafa Ali Hodjic and Redjo Ali Hodjic. Thes were the people that I knew very well. I saw them leave the camp and the rest I did not know so well or I did not recognise them. Dragan was yelling and there were other Serbian solders who were with Dragan, so it was difficult to register everything, but I knew that he said he was taking 12 men who will go and cut grass. So he started pointing at them and selecting them, but these were the ones that I recognised. That is all.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Smajlovic. Thank your, Honours. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you, madam. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you. Madam Smajlovic, while you were at the camp did you see any women working in the guard house washing dishes, making coffee, cleaning the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were washing the dishes. This was done by Sija Zepcanin and Biba Hadjic, these two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the camp were you physically mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, women were not mistreated, none of them, only this old woman that was once tied by Nikolic because she asked to go to the toilet when it was not the time to go. JUDGE ODIO BENITO: Thank you, madam. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mrs. Smajlovic, you were in the same hangar or camp with the men. Were you mixed or was there a barrier between the men and women in such a way that you had your intimacy reserved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. We were together in the same hangar but men were at one side and we were on the other side, women and children, but there was no barrier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in fact, you were living together, you could see eac other in every way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes, we could. That is true. We could see each other and we saw the whole room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were treated like men, I mean, using the toilets and all that sort of thing, you had to do it in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We had to use the buckets. There was a corner and there were actually two corners, and we women were a bit ashamed. There were men there, my brothers were there, my sons were there, children and all people from Vlasenica and the surrounding area, and they were all younger people. So there were only a few people my age, the rest were younger people. I would call them like my children, you know. So I was ashamed and there were other women who were very embarrassed, but we had to do it and what we did was we took a blanket, and then one would be holding the blanket and the other would be doing, urinating or whatever. So the blanket was put there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were taken in a truck, all of you, to the camp. When you were taken in the truck and you said there were 20 women and children and so on to the camp of Susica, how did they choose you? Were they choosing certain people and leaving others or just collecting anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they took us to the camp, you are asking about our being taken to the camp, or when we were leaving the camp? Are you asking about the arrival in the camp? I did not .....

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very first taking of people to the camp. Whom were they taking exactly? Were they taking only Muslims o were they taking the opposition or people who fought against them? What was their determining criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, they were collecting only Muslims, only Muslims. This was the only criterion and there was no other criterion, just being a Muslim or not being a Muslim. That was the only thing for them. They did not worry who he was, whether he was -- what their occupation was. The important thing was that he was a Muslim or she was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that nobody would talk to you because there was an order that nobody would talk to Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was true. They did not -- they were not allowed to talk to us. No Serb or a Serb woman, man or woman, were not allowed to talk to us Muslims. My neighbours, next door neighbours, would pass and I would say: "Good morning" when I saw them or "Good afternoon" or "Good evening" or whatever. They would just lower their heads and would not even answer my greeting, "Good morning" or "Good evening". They would just lower their heads and pass as if they had never seen me before while they had used to drink coffee with me, we used to have chats together. We were very good friends, but I do not blame them, you see. They were acting on some kind of orders, prohibition orders, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this start exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That started on 21st April when the JNA entered Vlasenica and when they captured Vlasenica. Up to that date everything was nice and fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the camp you said that Nikolic would choose a man an beat him and he would die later inside the hangar like Dedic and Music. What made him choose these people, in particular? Did they have a special role in the community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they had no special role at all. They were nice, fine people but they were Muslims and that, I think, was the only reason. They did not choose anybody in particular, just Muslims, and they took them one after the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were packed in the truck after leaving the camp, you said that they stopped the truck and they selected girls between, like, 15 years old, 16 years old, and there was -- they took 27 young women. What did you hear about these women afterwards and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not a word was ever heard from them. Nobody ever heard from them after that. We do not know whether they exist at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you said that you heard the soldiers saying, and I quote you: "We want Muslims to see how our seed is"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right. That is exactly what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is all you heard after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is all. That is all. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mrs. Smajlovic, let me assure you I am not going to put many questions to you, but you stayed in Susica camp for some 20 days; the men went out to work in the forest. What were the women doing meanwhile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing special. We just stayed in the camp. We did not do anything. They did not force us to do anything, to work. We just sat there

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The children in the camp, what did the children do? Children like to play, they like to run around, keep busy. So what was that like for the children in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the children just sat down. They were not allowed to move around. They were with their mothers sitting in their laps, and they brought, according to Nikolic's orders, Sija Zepcanin she used to bring milk to children, a biscuit. Then for lunch they also had some food, the same food as we had. In the evening for dinner children received a cup of milk or a biscuit or if they had some spare bread they would give them a slice of bread. I also received some food from guards when Nikolic was away. They would give us either some milk to us elderly women. I was very weak at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you have moved to where you are now, have you seen any women survivors of that camp? Have you talked and what can you tell us on that score?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not talk to them a lot. I know several women but I seldom visit them. I live away from them. I do not like to walk around too much. I am not really fit. I have problems walking around. So I did not have many conversations with them, but Dika Zubovic was there and Fadila Karavic. She lives in Gracanica and that is far from where we are. Then there was this woman Kicic, she lives in Tuzla but, you know, you have to pay for the ticket and visit her and I do not have any money so I cannot see them very often. So I did not have many conversations with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went through that some three years ago now. You are at the International Criminal Tribunal which one da should listen to the defence. Now I would like to know, to finish, what your feelings are about all you have lived through. Do you feel hatred, sadness, a feel of revenge, disgust?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel -- let me try to tell you. I feel that had my son done something like that and had I seen it with my own eyes, I would have testified against him as I am testifying against Nikolic. I would not be sorry because I would ask punishment for my son if he had done anything like that, because this was pure hatred and the only reason was to try to destroy the Muslim nation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you, Mrs. Smajlovic. The Tribunal is very appreciative for you having testified. We realise it was not easy for you. You will be seen out. You will be cared for by the witness people. We hope you will have a safe journey home to your new home, and we do hope that you will find the piece of mind you deserve in the future thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Original in Bosnian] Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, that concludes the evidence we wish to call from the eyewitnesses themselves. We have previously provided your Honours with the documentation that was placed in support of the indictment, plus additional material. The statements from witnesses who were not called at these proceedings, we would ask your Honours if the order for non-disclosure that has been issued could be applied to those statements. But in order to give some evidence o the contents of some of those statements, we would seek to call an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor's Investigation Section, Investigator Paepen. He, if your Honours please, will give some evidence of the contents of some of the more of the important statements that are submitted in support of the indictment. Subject to your Honours' order, Investigator Paepen will not make reference to the names, addresses or any other identifying material contained in the statements. He will merely give a brief summary, if your Honours please, of the contents of the more significant of those statements. Subject to your Honours' orders, I will then seek to call Investigator Paepen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] With regard to the orders, the Registrar perhaps can tell us exactly what the situation is. We had an order for partial non-disclosure, so Mr. Paepen is going to testify publicly with full disclosure of his own identity. So we will keep the order, except that as far as this person goes we will lift it but we will keep for the testimony. So we will lift it for Mr. Paepen but we will maintain the order for the testimony that will be referred to. Is that right? Can you agree with that, Mr. Prosecutor? I admit it is a bit complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not entirely. Your Honour, Mr. Paepen's evidence, what he will give and what he will say, is contained in the statement. We do not seek that the non-disclosure order apply to that. We merely seek that the non-disclosure order apply to the statements themselves and to the names and addresses of the witnesses contained in those statements, but what he says is fo public disclosure. Just before I call Investigator Paepen, your Honours, there is a statement which we will refer to and is listed by the number 7.15. That is a statement by a witness of the Prosecutor and the Prosecution will no longer rely upon, and we ask that that be specifically excluded from the material in support of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Mr. Registrar, please. Yes, 7.15 I am not acquainted with, but if you have decided to withdraw that from the file that is fine. When we take the overall decision we will rule on this matter as a whole. Simply as you said, the statement was among the documents that had been provided to the Judge for confirming the indictment. That statement was in the indictment under Rule 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Now you are asking that it be withdrawn. We will take a decision on that, but we will tell you what the decision is when we take the final decision on the case as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] With regard to Mr. Paepen's testimony he is an investigator; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] So the Registrar is going to draft a decision to submit. So that everything be perfectly clear to everyone, Mr. Paepen is not a victim. He is here summoned by the Prosecutor in the same way as Dr. Gow was. So he is an investigator. He is going to testify publicly in line with Rule 61. So unlike the othe witnesses who were victims and did not want their addresses known, Mr. Paepen is going to be mentioning a number of names and it is in respect of those names that the Prosecutor is asking us to see to it that they remain confidential, that they are not disclosed. So now it is a matter for the Registrar to come up with the appropriate order. It is a bit complicated but we know the Registrar will be able to do it. One last question for you, Mr. Prosecutor. The wish of the Tribunal, but it is only a wish, we will hear out all the witnesses, and as you can see we are quite attentive, but the wish of the Tribunal would have been for us to finish by the end of the morning in hearing testimony. If that is not possible we can go on this afternoon. Did your office then plan to make a statement just so that we can organise our work for today? You have the floor sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My colleague, Miss McHenry, will wish to make a statement to your Honours in conclusion. I cannot be certain that Mr. Paepen will finish in an hour, but I will endeavour to move him along with such speed as I can muster to achieve that end. Your Honours, in relation to something that fell from your Honour, Mr. Paepen will not mention the name of the witnesses. He will refer to them by reference to the statement number in your Honours' dossier. In fact I hand to your Honour the list of references that Mr. Paepen will relate to. Your Honours, will see the statement number and your Honours will see in the right-hand column -- sorry, the right-hand column is the list o numbers and in the right-hand column is the actual names. It is those names that we are seeking to be kept confidential. When Mr. Paepen refers to the number your Honours will see the name to which he is making reference, which is the statements that are contained in your Honours' dossier. At the conclusion of his evidence he has the statements which he can submit to your Honours for the record if that is required, but those statements are statements that are already in your Honours's dossiers. As I said, this is not all the statements. This is just a selection of the more important ones. There are numerous other statements which your Honours have already had access to and no particular reference will be made to those.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Maybe when we listen to Miss McHenry we could go into this. Just to make things clear, under this Rule 61 hearing that is coming to an end can we take it that the Prosecutor's Office thinks the major testimony is in this list which will remain confidential, and then the testimony we heard physically?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and all the other statements as well, but rather than go through every statement and have every statement summarised, which would take probably two days, it is better, we thought, just to rely on the most important statements, but we do seek to rely on all the statements when it comes to your Honours considering evidence at the conclusion of the matter. This is merely a selection that we have made based on our assessment of what we think are the most important witnesses and it is done this way in order to do it a quickly and as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Last question, Mr. Prosecutor, but it is more for your colleague now. I understand from Mr. Paepen, we are not going to restrict him in this way, he should say what he has to say, but it is just a view to organisation. Miss McHenry, maybe you can tell us how, long do you plan to speak in your conclusion since there should not be any questions, just a few questions, just a rough idea?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would estimate it would be approximately between half an hour and 45 minutes, although obviously I will take your guidance on that matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Fine. I believe we can call Jozef Paepen. Mr. Jozef Paepen, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Can you hear, Mr. Paepen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] So if you could kindly read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] You have the floor, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Paepen Jozef.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a citizen of what country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Belgian citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your current occupation

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1st July 1994 I worked as an investigator in the Office of the Prosecutor, of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to that what was your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was an officer of the Belgian Military Police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In July of 1994 were you part of a team assigned to investigate certain incidents relating to a particular camp at Susica in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very quickly, for the benefit of their Honours, can you tell them how you went about that process of investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as we got the assignment we got information and gathered information from the media, non-government organisations, Bosnian authorities. From this information, sir, we got the witnesses's names and then we started to interview different witnesses. When I interviewed most of those witnesses of course we got access to more names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and your team then proceeded to take a series of statements from these witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you for the purposes of giving your evidence today prepared a summary of some of those statements, in particular the statements that you considered to be the more important of all of the statements that were taken in relation to this investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, we selected 14 statements for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is 14 out of some 50 odd statements; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Prosecuting Counsel, excuse me, regarding these documents, will they be made available to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They have already been made available to the Tribunal, your Honour. The statements have, but I think Mr. Paepen has further statements, further copies of them. The copies have already been made available. They are the original dossier.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes, the original dossier contains all the testimonies, 7.46, and all the rest of them, but the testimonial made before the Tribunal which will be part of the transcription, as is the case for all the other testimonials, but as part of the written version, will the witness be able to deliver his document to the Tribunal or is it just a personal document that he possesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour, he has prepared notes to assist him in giving the evidence as expeditiously as possible. Those notes are not in a form I would imagine would be of assistance to anyone except the witness, but if your Honours wish to have the notes I do not think there would be any difficulty in them being made available, but he will be referring to them in order to assist him to organise his evidence, in a manner to assist him to deliver it as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] As far as I am concerned, I am not asking for the personal notes of the witness. I was just referring to what we did with Dr. Gow, because Dr. Gow did submit a type of memorandum, a type of written note. If this does not apply to the present witness we will not insist on this point. I was just raising the question, regarding the question of whether, in fact, Mr. Paepen ha produced some sort of memorandum; if not, there is no problem, Prosecuting counsel, and I will not pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, he has not prepared one. He has not prepared a formal statement, in other words. (To the witness): Mr. Paepen, when you refer in the course of evidence to particular statements how is it that you intend to identify the statement for the benefit of their Honours so they know which one you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The statements will be referred to by the number of reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Starting, firstly, with the first statement, can you proceed to give a summary of those statements that you have specifically selected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The first statement is the statement which is referred to under No. 7.27. This statement is of a 40 year old witness from Vlasenica who is a mechanical engineer. It is a statement about general information about the situation in the city of Vlasenica until the takeover by the Serbs. The witness states that during the elections, the multi-party elections, in 1990 he was elected and, as a result of that, he was elected President of the Executive Council in the city of Vlasenica. In the city of Vlasenica there was a parliament which consisted of about 60 people. 27 of those delegates were Serbian, 26 were Muslims from the SDA party and seven were from the opposition. From this parliament an Executive Council was constituted. The Executive Council was composed of six people from which our witness was the President. Beside the President there were two other Muslims and there were then three Serbian. Our witness states that he being the President of Executive Council which are Muslim -- I am sorry, I have interference -- as I told, the President of the Executive Council, he was a Muslim. The Mayor was Serb. The President of the police was also a Serb. In the city this police was composed of about 170 reserve policemen. About 110 of these people were from Serbian nationality, the others Muslims. Our witness sent messages to the national authorities, and the national police authorities urged the local authorities to change the number in order that the two ethnic groups would be represented as they were in number, that means around 50 per cent for each. However, the witness states that the police chief and the mayor, both of Serbian nationality, they did not comply with the situation and the request of the national police authorities. The witness states further on that prior to the war irregular military units were formed in the area of Vlasenica. This matter he put to the national government in Sarajevo, and he had several meetings with the military JNA command of the troops who were based in a city Han Pjesak which is not so far from Vlasenica. The Serbian soldiers were arresting Muslim people, and when the witness made this available, these remarks to the Serbian Colonel, the answer was just simple: "You know, they are soldiers. Things like that can happen." In order to try to change this, and the witness asked th Colonel that Muslim people would be also be allowed to be a part of those irregular troops and put them under one command. This demand was refused by the Colonel who told that Muslims were not allowed to have weapons because if they would have weapons they would shoot at the Serbs. Later on, the witness says that in his function as President of the Executive Council a lot of Serbs came to his office and they believed that he was a Serb mayor. They came to him and they made complaints, asking him why they, as Serb civilians, Serb citizens, did not yet have received the weapons, because a lot of the other Serb people had already received weapons. As he said: "But who delivered the weapons?" The answer was that the weapons were delivered by the army. Another incident in the beginning of the month of April 1992, the witness together with the Serb mayor went to a spot where a shooting had taken place. When arrived at this place, he saw several Serb children carrying weapons. When he asked them: "How do you come to those weapons? Where do they come from?" they said they were given to them by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that he speaks also in his evidence about a Crisis Committee being established, does he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He gives general evidence about the background of what happened leading up to and continuing on immediately after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you move on to the next witness now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, sir. The second witness is referred to unde No. 7.1. This witness is a 59 year old lady. The lady was not in the camp, but her daughter-in-law and 12 year old grand-daughter were in the camp. In order to be able to move into the city of Vlasenica and to go from the place in the city where she lived to the camp, which is only a few hundred metres away from her home to the camp, she needed a passport, a kind of laisser passer. This laisser passer was to be asked at the city authorities. She got one and we got the document in her possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A copy was made available during the course of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our next witness is referred to under the No. 7.33. The witness is a female witness, 60 years old, whose son was in the Susica camp. The witness says that after the takeover by the Serbs, immediately people, Muslim people, were arrested. First of all, the young men; some of them were sent back to their homes and then they were arrested again. The witness says that at the takeover, the Hodja, the Imam, had to tell the people to turn over the weapons. After that Serbs started looting the houses. This continued during the months May and June, and at the end of the month of June her son was arrested at her home. A few days later she was arrested. When she arrived at the camp she found back her son, her son who had been severely beaten up. I quote the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: camp to Batkovic, I heard my son, Fikret, asked to Dragan Nikolic if he could go with them. Nikolic yelled: 'You do not talk' and he put his bayonet in Fikret's mouth. The bayonet stayed in my son's mouth. My son was allegedly not wounded by the bayonet because I did not see any blood at this moment, but I was not able to talk to my son before I left the camp. When I left the camp my son Figret was still able to walk. I believe this his shoulder was broken because it was badly swollen. The right side of his face was swollen. His right eye was closed." End of the quote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the next witness?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next witness is a 63 year old man. The statement is referred as a No. 7.2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in summary form what can you tell us about this statement?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: In summary form, sir, this man has been arrested while working at the field. He was working together with his daughter. He was arrested by four men who were wearing the JNA uniform. This happened on 1st June 1992. He was brought to the Susica camp where he was interrogated first time, then a second time. During this interrogation he had been beaten and assaulted with a rifle butt. Three or four days after his arrival at the camp Dragan Nikolic, the camp commander, whom he knew personally because he had worked with his father, told him to give him all the valuables, money, jewels also ID cards with the promise that they would receive it back later on, but they never received it back. The witness names a few of the camp guards and during his stay he was a witness, he saw some people who had been beaten and who died as a result of the beatings

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he name those people?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What names are they, the ones that he saw killed?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The ones that he saw killed were Handzic, Durmo, Asim Zildzic, a man called Zekic, Kolarevic and then two other people whose name he does not know. During his stay at the camp our witness also witnessed the incident with the bayonet when the camp commander put the bayonet in the mouth of the victim Arnaut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Prosecuting counsel, if we could pay attention to one particular point here regarding confidentiality. You have just mentioned this incident of the bayonet and you mentioned the name of somebody. We have, in fact, concealed the name of the sister. I would like to point that fact out because we do have to pay attention to this particular question. Do you agree with that, Prosecuting counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
