utterances.text: I do, your Honour, and I would ask the witness to be careful about that. (To the witness): When you are giving answers would be careful not to .....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I will. The next witness, your Honour, is a female, 70 year old witness. The statement is referred to under number 7.6. In the summary this witness was taken out with the rest of the people from her street around 24th June to the Susica camp. She witnessed that detainees were beaten by Serb soldiers. Also this witness witnessed some people who died as a result of the beating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name those people that she witnessed being killed

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: Yes, she witnessed the killing of the people named Dzevad Saric, Mevludin Hatunic and a man called Ismet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she make any observations as to who carried out in whole or in part the activities in relation to these killings?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: This witness says that killings were done and the beatings were done by Nikolic, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to say in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: This witness has personally been beaten by Dragan Nikolic, the camp commander, and as a result of that there have been established medical documents at her return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next witness? The next witness, sir, is under the statement, refer No. 7.34. It is a 64 year old factory worker. The man lived in Vlasenica and after all the events that happened in Vlasenica he decided to escape. Together with a neighbour he tried to escape through the woods but on the date of the 12th July 1992 he was arrested in a village of Zeravic. From there they were brought to the local village and then they were brought to the SUP building, that is the police building in Vlasenica. In this building the witness has been beaten severely, interrogated, and he states that his teeth were beaten out. Then from this police building the witness has been brought to the Susica camp where at the day of his arrival and the day after the witness saw die two people. One -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the names of those people?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One was the name Music -- he did not know th first name -- and the second one is Galib Music.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he make any observations as to who participated in or carried out these killings?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: This witness, sir, it was the day of his arrival. The people were laying inside of the building and he did not see the beating himself. He just saw the people laying there and dying as a result of the beating and the lack of care.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next statement?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next statement is a 40 year old carpenter. The statement is referred to under No. 7.35. Again this witness has been arrested while working at his field. The day that he was arrested was 2nd June. The man was brought also to the Susica camp. In this camp he personally also witnessed the death of several people, people who died as a result of beatings by camp personnel or by the camp command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got the names of those?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The people who were beaten and who died as a result of those beatings were Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he also observe an incident in relation to the person called Cece Arnaut?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he did. He was also a witness on 30th June when the commander Dragan Nikolic put a bayonet into the mouth of that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next statement?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next statement is a statement of a 33 year old housewife. This statement is referred to under No. 7.37. This witness lived in a neighbourhood of Vlasenica and she was there together with her two children, a son of 11 and a daughter of five. Because of the events and attacks in the area they decided to run to the woods but they were arrested, and they were brought to the Susica camp where they stayed for about 20 days. She says in the camp men were separated from the women, no proper toilet facilities, no food during the first days. She says that Dragan Nikolic who she knew from before, because she was a brother's working colleague, was in charge of the camp. This witness saw the killing of three people: Mevludin Hatunic, Galib Music and a man called Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next witness, sir, the statement of the witness who is a 30 year machinist in an enterprise. This man -- I am sorry this statement is referred to under the No. 7.10 -- this man is from the village of Papraca where he was a member of a political party, President of the SDP, Social Democrat party. The witness states that in the period of 4th April 1992, also in Papraca, ultimatum was given to the Muslims in order to hand over the weapons, and they had the time to do that until the 8th April. Many Muslim people fled immediately after the ultimatum, but a few days later, since everything seemed to be calm, they returned, also our witness did. On 31st May 1992 all people were ordered to get at a particular place from where they were taken to the Vlasenica school. They stayed for about eight to nine days in the school and then they were transported to the Susica camp in Vlasenica The witness recognised Dragan Nikolic as the camp commander. Nikolic told the prisoners that he was the commander. During his stay in the camp he witnessed the beating of Durmo Handzic by Dragan Nikolic and the witness states that Handzic died the next morning. Also, the witness states that during his stay in the camp people named as Zekic Kolarevic and Ferhatovic -- excuse me, Ferhatbegovic were taken out. Then the witness heard shots and the people were never seen again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next witness, a statement referred to as the No. 7.19, a 31 year old shoe factory worker from the village of Papraca. On 31st May the witness was arrested while working in the fields and brought also then from his village to the school in Vlasenica. Around 8th June he was brought to Susica camp. The camp commander was Dragan Nikolic. The witness states also that the following people were badly beaten and died as a result of the beating: Durmo Handzic, Asim Zildzic. Further on during his stay in the camp, Muharim Kolarevic, Dzevad Saric, Zekic and Rasid Ferhatbegovic were called out and then the witness heard screams and gun shots. The witness states that he did not hear Nikolic that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next witness is a statement referred under the No. 7.41. It is an 18 year old female student who lived in Vlasenica and was taken prisoner together with her mother, two sisters and brought to the Susica camp on 1st July. Dragan Nikolic whom she knew from before the war was the camp commander 1 During her stay until 22nd July, she remembers that a man called Mevludin Hatunic as being interrogated and beaten by Dragan Nikolic. She says that when Hatunic came back, his face was swollen, he was vomiting blood and he died. Also the man Galib Music was taken out and beaten by Nikolic. A few days later this man died also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next witness?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next witness statement referred to as No. 7.42, a 36 year old driver from Vlasenica. The witness states that the Serbs issued an ultimatum to the Muslims to hand over their weapons, and this was in April 92. He was arrested on 2nd June with the other man, women and children from his street and he was taken to the Susica camp. He states that upon arrival at the camp their belongings and documents were taken by the Serbs. Nikolic Dragan was in charge of the camp, and the witness knows him because he is a former working colleague of him in the Alpro factory in the Vlasenica. Between the 20th and 25th June his brother and another man were called out by Nikolic and they were severely beaten. When his brother came back he had a wound at his cheek and seven of his ribs were broken. Another of the witness's brothers was also severely beaten several times. The witness further on states that Durmo Handzic, Asim Zildzic, Esmir Smajlovic and Mirsad Smajlovic were taken out by Nikolic and severely beaten. Both Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic died as a result of the beatings. The witness states that when Asim Zildzic returned into the hall, or was brought back into the hall, one o his eyes was out of the socket. A few days later after the killing of those people, the witness states that Muharem Kolarevic, Dzevad Saric and Zekic were taken out. The witness states that he heard then cries and some shots. This witness also recalls the incident when the camp commander, Dragan Nikolic, put the bayonet in the mouth of one of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of that prisoner?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: I am sorry, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of the prisoner who he saw put the bayonet in the mouth of?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The man, the name is Arnaut Cece, "Cece" is the nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next witness?

utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the
utterances.text: The next witness is the statement is referred under the No. 7.13. The witness is a 43 year old construction site worker from Vlasenica. He knew personally Dragan Nikolic, the camp commander. During his stay into the camp the witness also witnessed the beating of Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic by Dragan Nikolic. utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that questions brings me to a further question, Mr. Paepen. We listened to 12 or 13 witnesses who were called by the Prosecution. Needless to say w listened to the witnesses as attentively as possible. utterances.speaker: "When the older men were transported from the

Concerning the numbers of the female persons in the camp, it is very difficult, it was very difficult to put exact numbers, this is the same for the male persons, because the witnesses who were available for us were taken in at different dates. We have witness statements of witnesses from different villages and different areas who were brought. As I told, people who came from Papraca who were absolutely not familiar with the people from Vlasenica, and who came in, they only knew their own people. They had their concerns about their own and they could not give much information about people from the other area Now, concerning female persons, a lot of them came in the camp, stayed there for, as I told, one or two days and were then moved towards the free territory. This is the general, also general conclusion of most of witnesses. A few women have been kept for a longer period, but most of the male witnesses who were in the camp between, let us say, the period of 2nd June and then transported towards the camp of Batkovic, it was three days at the end of June, 27th, 28th and 30th. utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. First, I would like to discuss a few preliminary matters. One is with the assistance of the clerk, we would like to submit some of the supporting documents for Dr. Gow's assertions that I believe Judge Riad, in particular, had asked and we had stated that, although we might not be able to submit every potential bit of support for his evidence, we would make submission of some of the important parts. utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Thank you very much, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: We would also ask at this time that all the documents that have been introduced in this hearing be formally admitted as evidence. I believe all those documents have previously during the course of the hearing been given to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] That is quite right. Yes, we approve that.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: With respect to your Honours' question immediately before the break about potential amendments, let me advise the court at this time the Prosecution is not seeking an amendment of the indictment. This is not to suggest at some future time, particularly in preparation for trial after the defendant is apprehended, I believe there would probably well be amendment sought at that time but at this time we do not believe it necessary or appropriate. With respect to the last matter raised by your Honours, which is a question directed at -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] So, Prosecuting counsel, let me turn to the Registrar before you start. Please note, Registrar, that the Tribunal registers the documents provided throughout the hearing as documents fully given to the Tribunal so that they may be perused and used as seen fit. Then, as procedural documents, please note th documents submitted during the testimony of Dr. Gow. We also register, we also note, that in this case against Dragan Nikolic we still have your indictment which has been confirmed by Judge Odio Benito under Rule 47 of our Statutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the last matter that you raised immediately before the break, a question, I believe, directed to Mr. Paepen which is whether or not there is some sort of final analysis of sort of everything. I do not believe that that there is such a document existing, although during the course of my argument, my closing argument, I will discuss why that is and what other things there are that do exist that might satisfy some of your Honour's concerns. If I may proceed? Your Honours, we have heard over the past five days some of the evidence against Dragan Nikolic. The case is a strong and simple one; one which illustrates often in frightening detail what happened. It does this by being a case about individuals. Certainly, it is a story of the individual witnesses who testified here this week who, with great courage and with great eloquence, came here and testified before the world. It is hoped that the voices of these witnesses will speak for other victims and serve as an aid to recovery and a remembrance of some of the victims who did not survive. As many of the witnesses' testimony established, this is also the story of some individuals, including some Bosnian Serb individuals, who with dignity and courage acted to help in some way their victims often at risk to themselves The individual this story is most about is Dragan Nikolic; a person in an official capacity; a person with responsibility over the lives of many; a person who permitted others and was permitted by others to kill, torture, assault and otherwise abuse detainees in the most horrible of ways. By speaking of individuals, I do not mean to suggest that Nikolic and his crimes were not part of something larger, because he was and his crimes were. What I mean is that even when crimes are done as part of something bigger involving other individuals, this Tribunal is about individual choices and individual criminal responsibility. War is tragedy. It inevitably involves suffering and death. It is not, however, an activity conducted without legal rules. These rules, International Humanitarian Law, exist to mitigate, where possible, human suffering during wartimes. These rules are universally recognised as establishing the outer limits of acceptable conduct. Murder, torture, inhumane treatment and the other crimes committed by Dragan Nikolic at Susica camp are prohibited at all times in all contexts. By bringing this case and now by bringing this Rule 61 hearing, we condemn all such violations of International Humanitarian Law and we put Dragan Nikolic and all other perpetrators and potential perpetrators on notice. No matter your position, high or low, no matter how famous or unknown your crimes may be, no matter what your nationality or ethnic origin, actions such as those taken here violate the most basic tenants of international law accepted by all nations. As such, you may b prosecuted, and the efforts to bring to light your crimes, and to bring you to justice, will not cease. Dragan Nikolic is accused here or imprisoning more than 500 civilians, of subjecting them to inhumane conditions, of plundering their property, and of sending many to another prison camp, where their suffering continued. His is also accused of killing eight of the detainees, of torturing 10 others and causing serious injury or great suffering to others. Dragan Nikolic was the camp commander at Susica. As such, under Article 7 of our Statute, he can be held culpable for both his personal participation in crimes, and for his responsibility as a superior who could have prevented or punished the crimes of those he supervised. The evidence showed that Nikolic ruled Susica with an iron hand. As he himself said to the detainees: "I am your God and your law". He was at the camp almost all the time. He controlled what went on at the camp and the actions of the guards. But rather than use his position to protect the basic rights of the detainees, imprisoned solely because they were Muslims, Nikolic permitted, nay he encouraged, abuse. He permitted the guards and he permitted others from outside the camp to assault, torture and even kill the detainees. He created, by his own example, an environment where sadistic physical and mental abuse of the detainees was common place. Under the law, Nikolic is thus responsible for the offences at the camp without the necessity of his personal participation. Additionally, however, in almost all, if not all, the cases of the charges in thi indictment, Nikolic is also responsible through his personal participation. I would like to briefly discuss the crimes charged in indictment one by one. I would also like to present the court with the assistance of the clerk with a chart detailing which witnesses had specific testimony relevant to a particular count. The chart that I am presenting may not include a reference to every witness with relevant testimony, but I hope it identifies the major witnesses with respect to each charge. By the term witnesses here, I use the term to include both witnesses who have testified this past week as well as the many more witnesses who have provided written statement and who will come to The Hague to testify at trial. As your Honours know, the Prosecution is relying on both the oral testimony and the written statements previously submitted in this proceeding. There are some crimes, in fact, where the Prosecution's evidence is entirely in the written material. What emerges from the witness who testified is a ghastly picture of the crimes and of the suffering experienced by the victims of those crimes. As we also saw during the hearing, that suffering continues, both with respect to the surviving victims, the witnesses to the crimes and the families of those who did not survive. Here I am going to try to summaries and synthesize the various witnesses' testimony rather than repeat the details of what every witness said. I do not believe it is necessary, or even helpful, for me to discuss the testimony of each witness. Not only is that evidenc already before your Honours, more importantly, the standard in this case is not proof beyond a reasonable doubt or even preponderance of the evidence. This proceeding is for your Honours to confirm that, taking into account all the evidence and reasonable inferences to be drawn, there exist reasonable grounds to believe that the accused has committed the crimes charged in this indictment. As stated by Judge Sidhwa, "The evaluation is to be made at the pretrial stage of the proceedings, and not what may turn out subsequently in the light of changing facts". Later: "The evidence, therefore, need not be overly convincing or conclusive; it should be adequate or satisfactory to warrant the belief that the suspect has committed the crimes". As a concrete example of the different standard for a Rule 61 proceedings as opposed to a trial, I would offer the following example. If I were to go into a room filled with several people and call out "Michelle", and of those persons turns her head, I would suggest that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the person who turned her head is Michelle. I do not suggest that the evidence of this is beyond a reasonable doubt, or even conclusive, because there are other plausible reasons which could explain what happened. I do submit, however, that it is evidence sufficient for a reasonable belief. Many of Dragan Nikolic's crimes were committed against, and in the presence of, people who knew him and his victims. Accordingly, in many cases the witnesses have vivid recollections of what happened during th crimes. As is natural, they often saw or heard different parts of the crime, and as is natural, particularly given the conditions here, the witnesses sometimes remember things differently. Indeed, it is remarkable that there are not more differences. But it is not necessary at this time, certainly not in these proceedings, to resolve any apparent inconsistencies. Although it is not necessary, or, I would suggest, even appropriate to try to resolve apparent inconsistencies at this stage, because your Honours have raised the issue, I would like to address this issue in more detail than I had originally planned. First, the Prosecution does not suggest (and has never meant to suggest) that it is inappropriate for your Honours to note inconsistencies. It is always advisable for the Prosecution to be aware of such issues and it is a natural human reaction of persons to wish to resolve inconsistencies, since when hearing a story one wants to understand it wholly and correctly. But, of course, it must be realised that there are different kinds of inconsistencies. Some may be the result of both the summary nature of the testimony that witnesses gave and the emotional nature of the testimony. It is also the case that the witnesses were not asked to clarify, or not sure that there was not a misunderstanding because of translation or other issues. It is also the case, as I believe has been previously pointed out, that the witnesses here were often at the camp at very different times. Mrs. Smajlovic came at th same time that many of the witnesses who testified earlier in the week were on the bus leaving. Mr. Pasic was there for only one night. There are other issues that, just because of the question involved are ones that the witness could never be expected to accurately know. I would suggest that some of what went on above Dragan Nikolic are some things that these witnesses may well not know. I would suggest that the number of the people in the camp is something that the witnesses would not be expected to know. The numbers were constantly changing. The conditions were such that it was hard and, even in the best of circumstances, it is a difficult task, certainly one that I believe I would never be able to estimate. We are sure, the Prosecution is sure, that it is at least 500 people, and that is what the indictment charges, a minimum of 500 people. We believe it was more than that, several thousand, but we have only charged a minimum of 500. So, I would respectfully submit that is all we need to know for sure. The other inconsistencies, the kind I mentioned before, are the result of the fact that all humans remember and see things differently. I have never had and do not know any Prosecutor who has ever had a case without inconsistencies; indeed, I would be suspicious if I were presented with such a case. So I think there are two important questions to keep in mind when thinking about such inconsistencies: (1) Do they go to an essential element of the offence? If not, they are much less serious and may not need to ever b resolved. (2) Are they of such a character that they render a witness not credible about the essential elements? I would respectfully suggest that in this case there are no inconsistencies whatsoever that come close to rising to these levels.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes. If I could just break in for a moment, just a slight break, we have a slight interpretation problem. (The Presiding Judge addresses Interpreters) Sorry to interrupt you, Prosecuting counsel. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honours, for all these reasons that I have just talked about, your Honours, I would notify you that the Prosecution does not have the summary that your Honour asked about, which is a summary that really, sort of, treats everything and resolves it as something close to the final answer. I will point out to your Honours that in the dossier that was initially received by Judge Odio Benito (and is now before your Honours) there is both an overview of Vlasenica and the camp. That may answer or, at least, give the Prosecution's belief as to some of the general questions, and with respect to the specific counts in the dossier there is also a section entitled "Allegations" which tries to summarise and synthesize the various witnesses' testimony -- similar to what I am going to try to do in just a minute myself. Your Honours, just as I will not discuss the testimony of every witness for similar reasons, I will not, unless your Honours desire it with respect to specific count, repeat the elements of the offence which Mr. Niemann previously described in his opening. I do have, however, for your Honours' consideration, if you desire it, copies of the Prosecution's submission on the elements of the offence that were submitted to the Tadic Trial Chamber. I have checked. They were previously submitted and they are part of the record in Tadic. They are currently being translated. My last information was that the French version will be available on Wednesday. I would like briefly to touch upon the jurisdictional requirements common to each of the offences under Articles 2, 3, and 5 of our Statute. Generally the acts committed by the accused here against specific victims have given rise to three separate charges: Grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions under Article 2, violations of the laws or customs of war under Article 3, they are specifically identified as being violations described in Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, and lastly crimes against humanity under Article 5 of our Statute. All of these require that there have existed an armed conflict. With respect to meeting this jurisdictional threshold, I direct your attention to the recent Appeal Chamber's decision in the Tadic case which found that an armed conflict exists whenever there is resort to armed forces, armed force between States or protracted armed violence between governmental authority and organised armed groups, and the additional finding that an armed conflict did exist in Bosnia-Herzegovina between at least the period 23rd May 1992 to 31st December 1992. I note that the indictment here against Dragan Nikolic fall completely within that period. I would also direct your attention to the testimony Dr. Gow and to the testimony of all the witnesses about the events occurring round Vlasenica, both of which substantiate the position that an armed conflict began in Bosnia-Herzegovina by early April 1992, that the conflict has continued, that the conflict in Vlasenica was closely related to the hostilities occurring in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, indeed, that the conflict in Vlasenica was part of a larger Vlasenica military campaign. With respect to Article 2, as also set out by the recent Appeals Chamber decision in Tadic, the conflict must be shown to be international and the victims must have been persons protected by the Geneva Conventions. Here we have more than established reasonable grounds to believe that this conflict was international. First, we had Dr. Gow's testimony indicating, among other things, that (1) in April and part of May there was a conflict between the independent State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the SFRY; (2) that at the conclusion of this period the newly constituted FRY left behind a conquering army in possession of much of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and (3) that the FRY continued to assist the forces of the Bosnian Serbs in a variety of ways. Further, in this case we had testimony from the witnesses from Vlasenica concerning the direct involvement of the Novi Sad Corps. from Serbia. Not only did the witnesses state that the Novi Sad Corps. was involved i the armed takeover of Vlasenica in April and May 1992, the witnesses also established that the Novi Sad Corps. provided continuing support to the local armed forces after this time by leaving significant amounts of equipment and weapons to the local Bosnian Serbs forces. Further, as stated by the Appeal Chamber's decision, International Humanitarian Law applies from the initiation of such armed conflict and extends beyond the cessation of hostilities until a general conclusion of peace is reached. Regarding whether the victims were protected persons, the testimony establishes that the victims, and indeed all the detainees at Susica camp, were civilians incarcerated solely because of their status as Bosnian Muslims. As civilians all the detainees are persons protected by the Fourth Geneva Convention of 12th August 1949 relative to the protection of civilian persons in times of war. Turning to the Article 3 charges, the Prosecutor must demonstrate that the acts or omissions of the defendant violate the wars and the customs of war. The accused here is charged under Article 3 with murder, torture and cruel treatment. As recognised by the Appeal Court's recent decision, such acts as these, described in Common Article 3, have been accepted as International Humanitarian Law applicable in all armed conflicts regardless of classification as internal or international. With respect to Article 5, crimes against humanity, the acts of the accused must have been knowingly committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against the civilian population. This has bee established here by Dr. Gow's testimony concerning the attack against non-Serbs in places throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, and by the witnesses' testimony concerning the fate of the civilian non-Serb population in and Vlasenica, and their own fate when later sent to other prison camps, including be Batkovic and Doboj. Among other things the testimony concerning the status of non-Serbs, in particular Muslims, around Vlasenica at that time included restrictions on movement, restrictions on employment, restrictions on the conduct of financial matters, forced deportation and the imprisonment and worse of civilians. Turning to the individual acts in the indictment, the first two counts in the indictment are based on the murders of Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic. Sometime between 13th and 24th June 1992 these two elderly men were called out of the hangar. After being called out they were savagely beaten by Dragan Nikolic. During the beatings Durmo Handzic was questioned about the whereabouts of his son, and Asim was questioned about a weapon. The men cried that they did not know the answers and they screamed in pain. They were beaten to unconsciousness and water was thrown on them to revive them and the beatings started again. During part of this event another detainee, Mirsad Smajlovic whom you heard testify yesterday was also called out and beaten for a portion of the time. When the beatings finally stopped, Durmo Handzic staggered back into the room and Asim Zildzic, unable even to walk, was dragged in by other detainees. Asim Zildzic died almos immediately afterwards. The following day, after being denied his last wish to be permitted to see the daylight outside, Durmo Handzic also diet. Count 3 of the indictment is the murder and wilful killing of Mevludin Hatunic. Mrs. Smajlovic testified about this crime and you have additional written material. The evidence indicates that the house of Mr. Hatunic had been taken over by a Serb family and Mr. Hatunic made some sort of negative comment about that. Dragan Nikolic found out about the comment and decided to punish Mevludin Hatunic for daring to make such a comment. The punishment was death. Over the next day or so Mr. Hatunic was repeatedly beaten by Dragan Nikolic and he died from his injuries. Count 4 to 7 of the indictment are based on an event involving four detainees: Dzevard Saric, Muharem Kolarevic, Musa Zekic, Rasid Ferhatbegovic. A number of witnesses have evidence about these murders, but perhaps the most chilling testimony came from Hasim Ferhatovoic who was called out during the incident and buried the victims and Ibro Osmanovic who was almost killed himself. The evidence reveals that late one night Mr. Saric, who had frequently been beaten by Dragan Nikolic before, was called out, as was Muharem Kolarevic. Some soldiers who were friends of Dragan Nikolic had come to the camp and they with Nikolic's acquiescence and participation led this incident. Detainees remaining in the hangar could hear beating, yelling and then some shots. Hasim Ferhatovoic and his brother Alija called Gitza were called out of the hangar, and when they found the two men both o whom appeared to be dead. Hasim and his brothers were ordered to move the bodies to another location and they did that. While they were still outside Musa Zekic, another detainee, was then ordered to come out of the hangar, and he too was killed. When the two brothers Hasim and Gitza were ordered to bring the body of Musa Zekic to the location where the other bodies were, it was discovered that Muharem Kolarevic was no longer there. Apparently, as it later turned out, he had been critically wounded rather than dead and he had managed to crawl some distance away before dying. In any event, because Muharem Kolarevic could not be immediately found, the soldiers raised a cry of escape. They then, accompanied by some police officers, went into the hangar and made the accusation that an escape attempt had been made. Ibro Osmanovic made the mistake of drawing attention to himself by slightly raising his head. He was picked as a person who tried to escape. One of the guards who had been a friend of his intervened on his behalf, and he was not taken and Rasid Ferhatbegovic was selected in his stead. Immediately after being taken out Rasid Ferhatbegovic was killed. Count 8 charges the murder of Ismet Dedic. Mrs. Smajlovic testified about his death and there is additional written evidence. Ismed Dedic was killed by being beaten to death by Dragan Nikolic. The witnesses do not know why Nikolic did this. They only know that he did it. Count 9 is the inhuman treatment of Galib Music. B way of clarification with this count I would like to add that although the evidence now indicates that Galib Music died from this mistreatment, because the state of the evidence regarding proof of death was not as clear when the indictment was first returned, Dragan Nikolic is not here accused of the death of Mr. Music, but only of inhumane treatment. Galib Music had the misfortune of having been a neighbour of Dragan Nikolic before the war, and he was accused of having been a supporter of the SDA, the Muslim party. Galib Music, a man in his 60s, was called out by Dragan Nikolic, and then while outside the witnesses could hear screams and Nikolic yelling. Sometime after Mr. Music was brought back to the hangar he died from his injuries. Counts 10 and 11 concern the assault Fikret Arnaut, called Cice. Cice was repeatedly, sometimes daily, assaulted by about Dragan Nikolic, often in the hangar in front other detainees Count 10 is based upon a particular incident where, as part of trying to obtain information or punish him, Dragan Nikolic forced Cece Arnaut to put back his head and Dragan Nikolic then put his bayonet down the throat of Cice, cutting him in the process. Count 11, charging great suffering, is based on the repeated beatings that Nikolic inflicted on Cice. Count 12 is the assault of Mubin Music. The evidence for this count is contained in the written material. Dragan Nikolic accused Mubin Music of knowing where a weapon, a Kalashnikov, was. In order to find out if Mubi Music knew where the weapon was and to force him to tell if he did, Nikolic assaulted Mubin Music by threatening him and also putting a bayonet down his throat. Counts 13 and 14 are the torture and inhuman treatment of Suad Machmutovic, a man Nikolic accused of having a vehicle with something on it resembling a Croatian flag. Suad Machmutovic testified during this hearing finishing yesterday morning. He told you about his beatings when Dragan Nikolic hit with a police baton, kicked him after he had fallen to the ground, beatings where he lost consciousness and beatings from which he still feels the affects. In addition to the physical beatings, Nikolic, while ordering Suad Machmutovic to provide information about a neighbour, put a cocked pistol in his mouth and pulled the trigger. Suad Machmutovic realised he was still alive. He realised the gun had not been loaded. Counts 15, 16 and 17 concern a series of three assaults committed by Dragan Nikolic and others against Sead Ambeskovic. Mr. Ambeskovic testified here earlier in the week. He was beaten the first day he arrived at Susica camp with axes, bars and rifle butts, and he was beaten the next day again with iron bars and other instruments. During the second beating he lost serval teeth and had his ribs broken. Two days later he was beaten again, this time with a baseball bat. Counts 18 is the inhuman treatment of Redjo Cakisic, another witness who testified during this hearing. He was beaten when he first arrived at Susica and again about 10 days later. On the second occasion Dragan Nikolic calle out Mr. Cakisic and brought him to two solders. Dragan Nikolic presented Mr. Cakisic to the soldiers and said: "Here, I have brought you something for dinner." The soldiers then bear Mr. Cakisic so badly that he could not stand up for seven days. While he was being beaten, while he was lying on the ground screaming and moaning, Dragan Nikolic continued his normal routine in the guard house some five metres away. The last count based upon an individual victim was the causing of great suffering to Hasna Cakisic. Most of the evidence supporting this count is contained in the written material. At the time she was brought to Susica Hasna Cakisic was 68 years old. She was at Susica camp for almost one month. While there she was brought out for interrogation serval times because Dragan Nikolic wanted to know where her son was, and during the interrogation she was slapped in the face and hit with the baton on her hand. Counts 20, your Honours, is the unlawful confinement of civilians and all the testimony attests to this. Count 21 concerns the appropriation of property. The refers to property including jewellery, money, watches, that the victims of Susica were forced to turn over and never received back. Count 22 is the transfer of civilians from Susica camp to Batkovic camp. Every male witness who testified reported that the men from Susica camp were transferred to Batkovic where they often remained detained for another 12 to 13 months. Count 23 charges Dragan Nikolic with committing crime against humanity by participating in the persecution of more than 500 civilians by maintaining the camp in which Muslims and other non-Serb people were detained based on the fact that they were Muslims. Count 24, the final count, charges Dragan Nikolic with a crime against humanity by participating in inhuman acts against the more than 500 detainees at Susica, by endangering their health and welfare by providing inadequate food, by providing living conditions failing to meet even basic minimal standards, and by creating an atmosphere where the detainees feared for their personal safety. This count is based upon the recognition that every person who was at Susica camp, even those themselves never beaten, were still the victims of inhuman treatment. Day after day these people were crowded on to a concrete floor, men, women, children, all together, no place to sleep, almost nothing to eat, no place to bathe, no place even to go to the bathroom. Every day these witnesses had to think about whether or not the next victim to fall prey to Dragan Nikolic, the next victim to be tortured or killed, might be them. This, your Honours, is the indictment. The evidence here more than establishes reasonable grounds to believe that the accused Dragan Nikolic committed all of these violations of International Humanitarian Law. I therefore ask your Honours to confirm all counts of the indictment and to issue an international arrest warrant for the arrest of Dragan Nikolic. If your Honours do confirm all or a portion of thi indictment, I would then ask for the opportunity to detail the Prosecution's efforts to gain custody over Dragan Nikolic, efforts which have been unsuccessful due to the failure of the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale to take appropriate action and arrest Dragan Nikolic. At that later time we would respectfully suggest that referral to the Security Council is appropriate. Your Honours, that is the conclusion of my presentation and, unless you have any questions, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] On the last point, Prosecuting Counsel, may I take it, along with my colleagues in the Tribunal, that you are blaming the refusal to co-operate on the part of a State, you are charging the lack of co-operation, you are asking that we take note of that and that the matter be referred to the Security Council? So you are referring to a State or to States?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am referring to a State as defined in our rules of procedure which state: A State as defined is a State member or non-member of the United Nations or a self-proclaimed entity de facto exercising governmental functions whether recognised as a State or not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes, fine. That was the answer I wanted you to give, so that we be certain that that is the request that you were putting to the Tribunal. The second comment I should like to make, by your leave, but I would like to hear what you have to say, having thus made your statement you consider that some of the major parts of the indictment, should the indictment be approved in it entirety. Under Rule 61C once the Tribunal has confirmed the indictment the Chamber will ask the Prosecution to read out the relevant parts and to give an account of the efforts made to gain custody. To my mind and my colleagues' minds that means that when we hand down our decision either we will confirm the indictment in its entirety or will confirm it only in part, but subsequently you will have to read out the relevant parts of the indictment. If we can confirm it is in its entirety, I take it that you might agree that the Tribunal would read that indictment, but that way you would not have to re-read what you have told us today. I would like to hear your view.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am in accord with you that that is what the Rules set out with respect to technically who -- I think it would be fine for your Honours to read it on our behalf and we would welcome that, in fact.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Even were it not confirmed entirely, we could still stick to that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I agree with you there also.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] These procedural issues, turning to those listening to us, this is an international jurisdiction, and we have to abide by international law. We want to set an example and we do have to respect our own rules. Each judicial step we take is a novelty for the Prosecution as well as for the Judges. I would like to hear your view on another matter. There is all the efforts that will have been deployed in respect of the confirmation by Judge Odio Benito. Have you provided us with the proof of the efforts? Let m make this clear, one of the purposes of this procedure is to make public -- that is why this is public -- the elements of the indictment against Dragan Nikolic, so to make these well known and also to deliver an international arrest warrant if we are convinced it is appropriate. But the Prosecutor's office has to tell us that the efforts have been made in terms of serving the indictment, and telling Dragan Nikolic that these proceedings are under way. So, do we have a document showing that these efforts have all been made or would you rather sum them up briefly now?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand the Rules, after your Honours have confirmed the indictment, under the Rules, the Prosection, but I think it would be the Prosecution could ask that the Trial Chamber do it on its behalf, a reading, in effect, shall describe the efforts made to have the arrest warrant served. This morning, your Honours, the Prosecution has asked the Registrar to submit to your Honours the Prosecutor's application that the indictment be submitted to the Trial Chamber, which includes an accounting of the efforts made by the Prosecution to have Dragan Nikolic arrested and to inform him of the charges against him. The supporting documents have also, I believe, been referred to your Honours. They are in both French and English. I would suggest that it is probably just technically more in keeping with the Rules to do it at the hearing in which your Honours indicate which, if any, portions of the indictment -- I have it in front of me if your Honours would like me to describe such efforts at the presen time?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Maybe we can do that at the hearing where we will be handing our decision. I will give you the floor on that occasion. You will go into the elements that would leave us to believe that you have done your utmost in terms of the serving the indictment, and either we will withdraw and deliberate, or whatever, we will take the decision then as to whether an international arrest warrant is appropriate. It may seem a bit lengthy, but we do want all these listening to us to understand what is involved. Do you have anything you would care to add?

utterances.speaker: MISS MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. With all due respect, and I do not mean to suggest for one minute that your Honours would not find that everything that we have done, that we have not done our utmost. I do not read the Rules to indicate that you are required to confirm the indictment to pass on the efforts made by the Prosecution, although it does appear that your Honours would have to do that under 61E in order to notify the Security Council. So, it is a sort of technical requirement because, we are assuming your Honours confirm all or a portion of the indictment, we do suggest that referral to a Security Council is appropriate. I would be asking your Honours to find that the failure to effect personal service was due in whole or in part to a failure or a refusal of a State to co-operate with the Tribunal. That is, in fact, why I asked the Registrar this morning to make you had all the supporting documentation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: [Original in French] Yes, we have taken note of that. That is quite true. The hearing relating to Rule 61 and th proceedings against Dragan Nikolic is closed. The Tribunal will be make its decision public, Friday 20th, at 11 o'clock. (The proceedings adjourned)
